Robbery
ROB-er-ee
n.
From rob, Old French rober, to plunder, of Germanic origin. Webster 1828: the forcible or felonious taking of goods from the person of another. Philippians 2:6 uses the Greek harpagmos, a thing seized or grasped at, in a construction that has been fought over since the fourth century.

Biblical Definition

Robbery appears in Scripture in three settings, and the third is one of the great Christological texts. In the psalm it is a warning against a whole way of getting: Trust not in oppression, and become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them (Psalm 62:10). Not merely do not rob — do not become vain in it, since the man who lives by taking begins to think of himself as clever rather than as a thief. In Isaiah it is worship built on plunder, which God says He hates: For I the LORD love judgment, I hate robbery for burnt offering; and I will direct their work in truth, and I will make an everlasting covenant with them (Isaiah 61:8). An offering funded by theft insults the God it is meant to honour. And in Philippians the word describes what Christ did not do: Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God (Philippians 2:6). Being in the form of God, equality with God was not a thing He had to seize, because it was already His — and the verses that follow describe Him laying aside not His deity but its manifest privileges, taking the form of a servant, and becoming obedient unto death.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ROBBERY as the forcible or felonious taking of anything from the person of another, or in his presence, against his will, by violence or by putting him in fear; and, more generally, the taking away by unlawful means what belongs to another.

expand to see more

ROBBERY, n. — The forcible or felonious taking of goods from the person of another, or in his presence, against his will, by violence or by putting him in fear.

In a general sense, the taking away by unlawful force or artifice what rightfully belongs to another.

Plunder; spoil; the thing taken by violence.

Figuratively, a seizing or grasping at what one has no right to hold.

From Old French rober, to plunder — the root also of rob, robber, and, through the sense of stripping, of robe.

Key Scripture

Psalm 62:10 — "Trust not in oppression, and become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them."

Isaiah 61:8 — "For I the LORD love judgment, I hate robbery for burnt offering; and I will direct their work in truth, and I will make an everlasting covenant with them."

Philippians 2:6 — "Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God:"

Proverbs 28:24 — "Whoso robbeth his father or his mother, and saith, It is no transgression; the same is the companion of a destroyer."

Modern Corruption

Philippians 2:6 has been made to carry a kenotic Christology in which the Son emptied Himself of divine attributes at the incarnation, and the Watchtower reads the same verse as proof that He never possessed equality with God at all.

expand to see more

The kenotic theories of the nineteenth century — Thomasius, Gess, and their English followers — took made himself of no reputation (literally, emptied Himself) in verse 7 to mean that the Son surrendered omniscience, omnipotence, or omnipresence in becoming man. This cannot stand with Chalcedon or with the text. Verse 6 says He was in the form of God and did not regard equality with God as a thing to be grasped at; verse 7 says He emptied Himself by taking the form of a servant. The emptying is an addition, not a subtraction: He took manhood, He did not lay down Godhead. A deity that can be set aside is not deity, and Colossians 2:9 says that in Him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily — present tense, of the incarnate Christ.

The Watchtower and other Arian readings run the other way, taking thought it not robbery to mean that Christ did not presume to grasp at an equality that was never His. But the clause is governed by being in the form of God, and the whole passage argues from what He was to what He was willing to become; there is no argument at all if He was a creature declining to overreach. Paul’s pastoral point in Philippians 2 depends on the height of the descent: the Corinthians are told to have this mind because the One who was equal with God took a servant’s form and a criminal’s death. Isaiah 61:8 supplies the practical corollary for the church — God hates worship funded by what was taken from someone.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek harpagmos (G725), a thing seized or to be grasped at; harpazo (G726), to seize by force; Hebrew gazel (H1498), robbery, that which is taken by violence; gazal (H1497), to tear away, to plunder.

expand to see more

Greek harpagmos (G725) — a thing snatched, or the act of snatching; the disputed word of Philippians 2:6.

Greek harpazo (G726) — to seize, to carry off by force; used of the catching up of the saints (1 Thessalonians 4:17).

Hebrew gazel (H1498) — robbery, plunder; I hate robbery for burnt offering (Isaiah 61:8).

Hebrew gazal (H1497) — to tear away, to seize violently; the root of gazel.

Greek kenoo (G2758) — to empty; made himself of no reputation (Philippians 2:7), the verb behind the kenotic controversy.

Usage

"Become not vain in robbery (Psalm 62:10) — the danger is not only the theft but the self-regard it breeds."

"I hate robbery for burnt offering (Isaiah 61:8) — worship funded by plunder insults the God it honours."

"Thought it not robbery to be equal with God (Philippians 2:6) — not a thing to be seized, because already His."
